title: Asking questions
description: Ask yes/no questions and questions with vad, var, vart, när, hur, varför, vilken and hur många, and answer with ja, nej or jo.

guide.summary: Swedish asks a question by moving the verb: first for a yes/no question, second after a question word. Learn the question words, the var and vart split, which agrees, and the special yes, jo.

sections.title: Yes/no questions: the verb goes first
sections.text: Swedish has no helper like English do. To ask a yes/no question, put the conjugated verb first and the subject straight after it.
steps: Find the conjugated verb: the one in the present or past form, or a modal like kan or vill.
Put it first.
Put the subject right after it; everything else stays where it was.
End with a question mark.
watch: Never add gör for English do: Gör du pratar is wrong.
An infinitive stays at the end: Kan du simma?

sections.title: Question word, then the verb
sections.text: With a question word, the question word takes the first place and the verb the second, just as in every Swedish main clause. The subject comes after the verb.
steps: Put the question word, with any noun that belongs to it, first.
Put the verb second.
Put the subject third, then the rest.
watch: Vad du heter is the order inside a longer sentence, not in a direct question.
A whole phrase such as hur många språk counts as the first place; the verb follows it.

sections.title: Var or vart: where, or where to?
sections.text: Swedish has two words for where. Var asks where something is or happens. Vart asks where to, with a movement towards a goal.
steps: Look at the verb.
If it means moving towards somewhere, use vart.
Otherwise, for a position or place of action, use var.
watch: English where to often drops the to; Swedish still needs vart.
Var is also the past of vara (was); the context shows which it is.

sections.title: The question words
sections.text: Each question word asks for one kind of answer. Learn them in pairs with the answer they expect.
steps: Think of the answer you want: thing, person, time, manner or reason.
Pick the matching word.
Then put the verb second.
watch: A name is asked with vad: Vad heter du? not vem.
Hur mår du? asks how you feel; hur är du asks what you are like.

sections.title: Vilken, vilket, vilka: which
sections.text: Which agrees with the noun after it, like an adjective: vilken for en-words, vilket for ett-words, vilka for every plural.
steps: Find the noun after which.
Plural? Use vilka.
Singular: en-word takes vilken, ett-word vilket.
watch: The gender of the noun decides, not the person asking.
Vilka covers plurals of both genders.

sections.title: Hur mycket or hur många?
sections.text: Hur mycket asks how much, for amounts you cannot count and for prices. Hur många asks how many, for things you count one by one.
steps: Ask yourself: can I count it one, two, three?
If yes, use hur många with a plural noun.
If no, or it is a price, use hur mycket.
Then put the verb after the whole phrase.

examples.en: How many languages do you speak?

watch: Hur mycket kostar asks the price; never use många there.
Mycket alone also means very or a lot.

sections.title: Answering: ja, nej or jo
sections.text: Ja and nej mean yes and no. Swedish has a third word, jo, for saying yes to a question with inte.
steps: Check whether the question has inte.
No inte: answer ja or nej.
With inte: jo contradicts it (yes, I do), nej agrees (no, I don’t).

examples.en: Don’t you speak Swedish? Yes, I do!

examples.sv: Har du en bil? Ja, det har jag.
examples.en: Do you have a car? Yes, I do.

watch: Ja after a question with inte sounds like agreement and confuses the listener.
Short answers repeat the verb with det: Ja, det gör jag.

steps: Find the conjugated verb.
Put it first, then the subject.
Leave the rest as it was and end with a question mark.
Put the question word or phrase first.
Put the verb second.
Put the subject after the verb.
Look at the verb.
Movement towards a goal: vart.
A position or place of action: var.
Decide what the answer would be: thing, person, time, manner or reason.
Take the matching question word.
Keep the verb second.
Find the noun after which.
Plural: vilka.
Singular: vilken for en-words, vilket for ett-words.
Can you count it one by one?
Countable plural: hur många.
Uncountable or a price: hur mycket.
Look for inte in the question.
No inte: ja or nej.
With inte: jo to contradict, nej to agree.

exercises.instruction: Turn the statement into a yes/no question. Write the whole sentence.

mistakes.why: That keeps statement order and only changes the punctuation. In writing, a Swedish question needs the verb first.
Swedish never builds questions with a helper like English do. The main verb itself moves to the front.

exercises.hint: Move the verb to the very front.
exercises.feedback: A yes/no question opens with the verb, and the subject comes straight after it.
exercises.explanation: Swedish has no do-helper: you swap verb and subject. Du pratar becomes Pratar du, and the full stop becomes a question mark.

exercises.instruction: Turn the statement into a yes/no question. Write the whole sentence.

mistakes.why: The verb is still after the subject; a written question puts it in first place.
Only the verb moves. The subject follows it directly, and the object stays at the end.

exercises.hint: Which word is the verb? Put it first.
exercises.feedback: Verb first, then the subject ni, then the rest.
exercises.explanation: Har is the verb, so the question opens with it: Har ni en hund?

exercises.instruction: Choose the word that starts the question.

mistakes.why: That gives du twice and statement order. The subject is already after the gap.
Swedish has no do-helper for questions. Gör du i Göteborg means nothing useful here.

exercises.hint: A yes/no question opens with the verb itself.
exercises.feedback: Put the verb in the first slot; du already follows the gap.
exercises.explanation: Bor du i Göteborg? asks Do you live in Gothenburg? The verb bor opens the question.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Statement order with a question mark only works in speech, with a rising tone.
The infinitive simma stays at the end. It is the conjugated verb, the one with -r or the modal, that moves.

exercises.hint: Which word should come first in a written question?
exercises.feedback: Swap the verb and the subject.
exercises.explanation: In a yes/no question the finite verb kan goes first and du follows: Kan du simma?

exercises.instruction: Build the question: Do you have a pen? Leave one tile unused.

mistakes.why: Gör means do or make. Swedish asks with the main verb, so this says Do you make a pen.
Statement order. Put the verb first to make a written question.

exercises.hint: No helper verb in Swedish.
exercises.feedback: Start with the verb har.
exercises.explanation: Do you have becomes Har du: the verb itself opens the question, and English do has no Swedish twin.

mistakes.why: Statement order. A yes/no question starts with the verb.
Tåget is an ett-word, so the adjective takes -t: the form without it does not agree.
Swedish says the train with the ending -et on tåg.

exercises.hint: Start with the verb for is.
exercises.feedback: Verb first, then the subject tåget.
exercises.explanation: Är opens the question and the subject tåget follows. Late is sent, agreeing with the ett-word tåget (försenat is also fine).

exercises.instruction: Write the verb bo in the right form.

mistakes.why: Bo is the infinitive. The question needs the present form with -r.
Du is already written after the gap. The verb comes before the subject in a question.

exercises.hint: After the question word comes the verb.
exercises.feedback: Question word, verb, subject: the verb is second.
exercises.explanation: Var bor du? The question word takes the first place, the verb bor the second, and du comes after it.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. The subject before the verb is the order inside a longer sentence, not in a direct question.
The question word goes first in Swedish, not at the end.

exercises.hint: The verb belongs in second place.
exercises.feedback: Question word first, then the verb, then the subject.
exercises.explanation: Vad heter du? means What is your name? The verb heter must come straight after vad.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: the subject has slipped in before the verb.
The question word belongs at the front of the question.

exercises.hint: Count the places: när is first, so what is second?
exercises.feedback: The verb must stand right after the question word.
exercises.explanation: Every Swedish main clause keeps its verb in second place. När fills the first place, so kommer goes next and bussen after it.

exercises.instruction: Build the question: How are you? Leave one tile unused.

mistakes.why: Hur är du asks what kind of person you are. For health and mood Swedish uses må.

exercises.hint: Swedes ask how you feel with må.
exercises.feedback: Question word, verb, subject.
exercises.explanation: Hur mår du? is the everyday way to ask How are you? Hur first, the verb mår second, du last.

mistakes.why: The subject came before the verb. After a question word the verb comes first.

answers: Vad är du gör i dag?
mistakes.why: Swedish has no are doing form. The simple present covers it.

exercises.hint: Question word, then verb, then subject.
exercises.feedback: Vad first, gör second, du third.
exercises.explanation: Vad gör du idag? The verb gör follows vad directly; Swedish uses the simple present for are doing.

exercises.instruction: Ask about the time with när. Write the whole question.

mistakes.why: Subject before verb: a direct question keeps the verb in second place.
The question word replaces the time, so the time should go.

exercises.hint: När replaces the time; then the verb, then the subject.
exercises.feedback: Drop the time, start with när and keep the verb second.
exercises.explanation: När börjar filmen? asks When does the film start? The verb börjar comes straight after när.

mistakes.why: Vart asks where to, with a movement towards a goal. A station lying somewhere is not moving.

exercises.hint: Is anyone moving, or is the station just somewhere?
exercises.feedback: Ligger describes a place, not a movement.
exercises.explanation: Var asks about location: Where is the station? Ligger is a verb of being somewhere, so no movement is involved.

mistakes.why: That asks where something is. With åka the question is about a destination, so the form for direction fits.

exercises.hint: Åka means travel. Is there a destination?
exercises.feedback: Movement to a place takes the form with -t.
exercises.explanation: Vart asks where to: Where are you going this summer? Åka is a verb of movement.

exercises.instruction: Write where or where to in Swedish.

mistakes.why: That form asks about position. Går du is a movement towards somewhere.
Vad means what. The question is about a place.

exercises.hint: Gå here means going somewhere.
exercises.feedback: Movement towards a goal needs the form with -t.
exercises.explanation: Vart går du? means Where are you going? With a verb of motion Swedish asks with vart.

exercises.instruction: Write where or where to in Swedish.

mistakes.why: That form asks where to. Working at a place involves no destination.
Vem means who. The question is about a place.

exercises.hint: Does the brother move towards a place, or work at one?
exercises.feedback: Working happens at a place: no movement.
exercises.explanation: Var jobbar din bror? asks Where does your brother work? Jobba is not a verb of motion.

answers: Vart ska du åka i morgon?
Vart ska du gå i morgon?

mistakes.why: That form asks about position. Going somewhere needs the word for direction.
After the question word the verb comes second, before du.

exercises.hint: Going means movement.
exercises.feedback: Use the direction word and keep the verb second.
exercises.explanation: Vart ska du i morgon? Movement to a destination takes vart; ska can stand alone in the sense of be going.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. That question word asks where something is, but åka has a destination.
Vad means what. The question is about a destination.

exercises.hint: Åker is a verb of movement.
exercises.feedback: Change the question word to the one that asks where to.
exercises.explanation: Åka means travel to somewhere, so the question needs vart: Where are you going on Saturday?

mistakes.why: Vem means who. With heter Swedish asks for the name with what, not who.
Hur means how. How is your teacher called is not how Swedish asks for a name.

exercises.hint: In Swedish you ask what someone is called.
exercises.feedback: Think of What is your teacher called?
exercises.explanation: Vad heter din lärare? Swedish asks for a name with vad, literally What is your teacher called?

exercises.source: ____ är du trött? Jag sov dåligt.

mistakes.why: När asks when. The answer is a reason, not a time.
That asks where. The answer says nothing about a place.

exercises.hint: The answer gives a reason.
exercises.feedback: Match the question word to the answer: a reason.
exercises.explanation: Varför means why. The answer I slept badly gives a reason.

exercises.instruction: Write the Swedish word for who.

mistakes.why: Vad means what. Who is it asks about a person.
That means which, and it chooses from a group. Here you simply ask about a person.

exercises.hint: The question is about a person.
exercises.feedback: Swedish who has one form.
exercises.explanation: Vem är det? means Who is it? Vem asks about people.

exercises.instruction: Write the Swedish word for when.

mistakes.why: That asks about a place, not a time.
Hur means how. The question asks for a time.

exercises.hint: The answer would be a time.
exercises.feedback: A time question.
exercises.explanation: När slutar du jobbet? asks When do you finish work?

exercises.source: How do you say this in Swedish?
answers: Hur säger man det här på svenska?
Hur säger man detta på svenska?
Hur säger man det på svenska?
Hur man säger det här på svenska?
mistakes.why: The verb must come before the subject after a question word.

answers: Vad säger man det här på svenska?
mistakes.why: Vad means what. How do you say asks with the word for how.

exercises.hint: How is hur, and the subject is man.
exercises.feedback: Question word, verb, subject.
exercises.explanation: Hur säger man det här på svenska? Swedish uses man (one) for a general you, and the verb säger comes second.

exercises.instruction: Build the question: Why are you laughing? Leave one tile unused.

mistakes.why: Vart asks where to. The question wants a reason.

exercises.hint: Why is one word in Swedish.
exercises.feedback: Question word, verb, subject.
exercises.explanation: Varför skrattar du? Varför means why, and the verb skrattar comes straight after it.

mistakes.why: That is the form for ett-words. Buss takes en.
That is the plural form, but the question is about one bus.

exercises.hint: Buss is an en-word, and there is one bus.
exercises.feedback: Match which to the noun after it.
exercises.explanation: Buss is an en-word in the singular (en buss), so which is vilken.

mistakes.why: That form goes with en-words, and rum takes ett.
That form is for several things. The question asks about one room.

exercises.hint: Rum is an ett-word.
exercises.feedback: Ett-words take the form with -t.
exercises.explanation: Rum is an ett-word (ett rum), so which room is vilket rum.

exercises.instruction: Write the Swedish word for which.

mistakes.why: That is the singular en-form. Böcker is several books.
That is the singular ett-form, and böcker is plural.

exercises.hint: How many books?
exercises.feedback: Böcker is plural.
exercises.explanation: Böcker is the plural of bok, and every plural takes vilka, whatever the gender.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. The en-form does not match an ett-word.
That is the plural form, but äpple here is one apple.

exercises.hint: Is äpple an en-word or an ett-word?
exercises.feedback: Make which agree with äpple.
exercises.explanation: Äpple is an ett-word (ett äpple), so which apple is vilket äpple.

mistakes.why: That form belongs to ett-words; färg takes en.
After the question phrase the verb comes next, before du.

exercises.hint: Färg is an en-word.
exercises.feedback: Which agrees with färg; then verb, then subject.
exercises.explanation: Vilken färg gillar du? Färg is an en-word, so which is vilken, and the verb gillar comes before du.

exercises.instruction: Replace film with filmer and make which agree. Write the whole question.

mistakes.why: Which still matches the singular. A plural noun needs the plural form.
That is the singular ett-form; filmer is plural.

exercises.hint: Several films.
exercises.feedback: Plural nouns take one form of which.
exercises.explanation: Filmer is plural, so vilken becomes vilka: Which films do you want to see?

mistakes.why: That asks how many and needs things you could count one by one.

exercises.hint: You are asking about an amount of money.
exercises.feedback: Price questions ask how much.
exercises.explanation: Hur mycket kostar biljetten? A price is an amount, so Swedish asks hur mycket.

mistakes.why: That word goes with amounts you cannot count, like water or time.

exercises.hint: Children can be counted.
exercises.feedback: Countable plurals take the word for many.
exercises.explanation: Hur många barn har ni? Barn here is plural and countable, so how many is hur många.

exercises.source: How much coffee do you drink?

mistakes.why: That asks how many, which needs countable things.
The verb comes straight after the question phrase.

exercises.hint: Coffee cannot be counted.
exercises.feedback: Hur mycket, then the noun, then verb and subject.
exercises.explanation: Hur mycket kaffe dricker du? Kaffe is uncountable, so hur mycket; the verb dricker follows the whole question phrase.

exercises.instruction: Build the question: How many languages do you speak? Leave one tile unused.
exercises.source: How many languages do you speak?

mistakes.why: That word is for amounts you cannot count. Languages are counted one by one.

exercises.hint: Languages can be counted.
exercises.feedback: Hur många språk fills the first place; then the verb.
exercises.explanation: Hur många språk pratar du? Languages are countable, and the whole phrase hur många språk stands before the verb.

exercises.instruction: Replace kaffe with äpplen and change the question word to match. Write the whole question.
exercises.source: Hur mycket kaffe vill du ha?
answers: Hur många äpplen vill du ha?
Hur mycket äpplen vill du ha?
mistakes.why: Apples are countable, so the word for an amount no longer fits.

answers: Hur mycket kaffe vill du ha?
mistakes.why: That is the original question: kaffe was never replaced.

exercises.hint: Apples can be counted.
exercises.feedback: Countable plural, so the question word changes.
exercises.explanation: Äpplen are counted, so hur mycket becomes hur många.

exercises.instruction: Choose the answer that means yes.

mistakes.why: After a question with inte, the plain yes is not used; Swedish has a special word that contradicts the negative.
Nej means no. The answer lite (a little) says yes.

exercises.hint: The question has inte in it.
exercises.feedback: A yes to a negative question has its own word.
exercises.explanation: Jo answers yes to a question with inte: Don’t you speak Swedish? Yes, a little.

exercises.instruction: Choose the answer that means yes.
exercises.source: Har du en cykel? ____, en röd.

mistakes.why: That word contradicts a negative question, and this question has no inte.
That means no, but the answer goes on to describe the bike.

exercises.hint: Is there inte in the question?
exercises.feedback: A plain question takes the plain yes.
exercises.explanation: Ja answers yes to a positive question: Do you have a bike? Yes, a red one.

exercises.source: Är du inte hungrig? ____, jag har redan ätit.

mistakes.why: That would mean Yes, I am hungry, which clashes with having eaten.
After a question with inte, ja is unclear and not used. The speaker means no.

exercises.hint: I have already eaten: hungry or not?
exercises.feedback: The speaker agrees that they are not hungry.
exercises.explanation: Nej agrees with the negative: Aren’t you hungry? No, I’ve already eaten.

exercises.instruction: Write the Swedish word for yes.
exercises.source: Kommer du inte i kväll? ____, jag kommer.

mistakes.why: That is the plain yes, used for questions without inte.
That means no, but the answer says jag kommer.

exercises.hint: The question has inte.
exercises.feedback: Contradicting a negative question needs a special yes.
exercises.explanation: Jo means yes after a question with inte: Aren’t you coming tonight? Yes, I am.

exercises.source: Don’t you live here? Yes, I do.
answers: Bor du inte här? Jo, det gör jag.
Bor du inte här? Jo, jag bor här.
Bor du inte här? Ja, det gör jag.
mistakes.why: After a question with inte the plain yes is not used for contradicting.

answers: Bor du här inte? Jo, det gör jag.
mistakes.why: Inte comes straight after the subject du, before the rest of the sentence.

answers: Gör du inte bo här? Jo, det gör jag.
mistakes.why: Swedish does not ask with a do-helper: bor itself starts the question.

exercises.hint: Inte goes after du; the yes is special.
exercises.feedback: Verb first, then du, then inte. Answer with the yes for negative questions.
exercises.explanation: Bor du inte här? Jo, det gör jag. Jo contradicts the negative; det gör jag is the Swedish for I do.

alternatives.answer: Bor inte du här? Jo, det gör jag.
alternatives.message: Right, and very common in speech. Bor du inte här? is the neutral written order.

alternatives.answer: Bor inte du här? Jo, jag bor här.
alternatives.message: Right, and very common in speech. Bor du inte här? is the neutral written order.
